captions.text: Defensiveness kicks in immediately.
Cognitive dissonance takes over.
The employee starts arguing about the specific context of
a minor event from six months ago.
Well, in February, the server was down.
Exactly. And the actual necessary performance
correction is completely lost in the noise and the
anger. By doing a one minute redirect instantly,
you deal with one specific behavior at a time
in a small, manageable dose.
I understand avoiding the gunny sack, but I have
a major issue with the execution of the redirect.
Okay, lay it on me.
If you do what the manager did with John
Levy, if you chew them out, tell them you
are legitimately angry, let them stew in that terrifying
silence, and then instantly pivot and tell them how
great they are and how much you trust them,
doesn't that just give them emotional whiplash?
It feels a bit jarring.
Yes. Doesn't the praise at the end completely dilute
the severity of the correction?
I'd imagine John walks out thinking, "Wow, he was
mad for a second." But then he said, "I'm
his best engineer, so we're all good.
No big deal." It seems counterintuitive, and a lot
of old school managers share your exact concern, but
behavioral psychology proves the exact opposite is true.
Let's look at ego preservation.
If you only attack, if you only reprimand the
person and leave it there, what does the
employee do the second they leave your office?
They go find their work best friend, go get
a coffee, and spend an hour complaining about what
an absolute jerk the boss is.
